summary: The note is a first-person account of a visit to Henderson Park on March 10th, 2024, arguing that urban green spaces are vital habitats for biodiversity. It draws on conversations with an ornithologist, a lepidopterist, an ecologist and a city horticulturist about birds, insects, water features and native plants. It closes by stressing human stewardship and environmental education in protecting urban wildlife.
one_line: A visit to Henderson Park and expert interviews show how urban green spaces support birds, insects, aquatic life and native plants, aided by community stewardship.
key_facts: The author visited Henderson Park, described as the city's "green lung," on the morning of March 10th, 2024.
Ornithologist Dr. Alice Morgan spoke with the author on September 15, 2023, saying urban parks are pivotal stopover points for migratory birds.

Dr. Morgan named the ruby-throated hummingbird and warblers as migratory species that rely on urban greenery, and said "Without urban green spaces, many of these birds would struggle to complete their epic migrations."
Resident birds such as robins and blue jays disperse seeds and control insect populations in the park.
Lepidopterist Dr. David Lee spoke with the author on September 30, 2023, about the importance of green spaces for pollinators facing alarming declines.
A cluster of milkweed plants in Henderson Park serves as a micro-habitat for monarch butterflies.
Dr. Lee said each garden and park contributes to a patchwork supporting varied invertebrates, which matter to human survival through pollination.
Ecologist Emily Rivers, who studies urban water bodies, was interviewed on October 11, 2023; she said ponds and streams provide amphibian habitat and filter urban runoff.
Rivers said even a small pond can host life from microscopic algae to green herons, and can act as stepping stones for aquatic species in the urban landscape.
City horticulturist Marcus Zhang, interviewed on November 20, 2023, has spent years curating the park's plant life to promote biodiversity.
Zhang said the park focuses on native species because they are already adapted to local climate and soil and best support local wildlife.
Educational signs and community-led conservation initiatives in the park inform visitors and encourage them to protect biodiversity.
The note concludes that urban green spaces like Henderson Park are a cornerstone of maintaining biodiversity within city limits.
